[Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: one or two?"}
For one quarter, on every passing down:

- **Before the snap, count the deep safeties.** One in the middle or two split wide? Say "closed"
  or "open" out loud *at the snap*. Then look at the details: how deep are they (12 to 14 means
  halves, 8 to 11 suggests quarters), how wide (outside the hash means halves)?
- **Look at one cornerback.** Press or off? Inside or outside shade? Eyes on the receiver or turned
  in to the quarterback? Press with eyes on the receiver leans man; off and turned in leans zone.
- **One second after the snap, check yourself.** Did the middle stay closed or open? Did the corner
  run *with* his receiver or *to a spot*? Did he bail? Did a "two-high" safety drop down into the
  box or the hole? Write down what it became.
- **On the replay, watch one underneath defender for one second.** To a spot (spot-drop), with a
  receiver from the start (man), or with a receiver after a beat (match)? Then find the ball: if a
  receiver was open, which zone was he in, and where were the nearest defender's eyes?

Live, the safeties are often out of frame at the snap; the high, wide replay angles (the closest a
broadcast gets to the [All-22](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-all-22) film coaches use) are the
best place to make the call and check it.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: off corners, one safety"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-cover3
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-8, ball in the middle. One safety (FS) 14 to 15 yards deep in the middle of the field; the strong safety (SS) and the nickel ($) about 5 yards deep, each a couple of yards inside a slot receiver; both corners (CB) 7 to 8 yards off with outside leverage, their shoulders turned in toward the quarterback. The safety and corners are ringed."
pr1 = Play(spread(), nickel(FS=(14.5, 0.5), SS=(5.5, 6.9), NB=(5.0, -6.9), LCB=(7.8, -16.3),
                            RCB=(7.8, 16.3), MIKE=(4.5, 1.6), WILL=(4.5, -2.4)), los=40, to_go=8)
pr1.highlight("FS", "LCB", "RCB")
fld = draw(pr1, lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 19.0))
widths(fld, pr1, -6.6)
plt.show()
```

**Is the middle of the field closed or open? Which coverage is most likely, and if the offense
runs four verticals, which receivers have the best chance?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Middle of the field closed, most likely Cover 3.** One safety, deep and in the middle, is the
MOFC picture, which means Cover 1 or Cover 3. The corners settle it: 8 yards off, outside leverage,
turned in to see the quarterback is the deep-third corner's alignment, not the pressed, square,
eyes-on-the-man look of Cover 1. The SS and nickel sitting inside the slots, rather than tight on
them, add to the zone lean: they look like the two curl-flat defenders, with the linebackers in the
hooks.

Against four verticals, Cover 3 has three deep defenders for four deep routes, so the **slot
receivers running up the seams** are the best bets: each seam runs into the lane between a corner's
outside third and the safety's middle third, and the lone safety can only lean toward one of them.
Pattern-matching versions of Cover 3 exist precisely to fix this, with the curl-flat defenders
carrying the slots up the seams ([Cover 3](06-03-cover-3-family.qmd)). The short throws are open
too: with corners 8 yards off, a hitch or quick out in front of them is there all day, which is
the trade a Cover 3 defense accepts. And remember the shell could still rotate at the snap.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: two safeties, close to the box"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-quarters
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10, ball in the middle. Two safeties about 10 yards deep, each roughly over a slot receiver; corners 7 to 8 yards off; the nickel ($) inside the left slot; two linebackers. The safeties are ringed."
pr2 = Play(spread(), nickel(FS=(10.0, -6.5), SS=(10.0, 6.5), NB=(4.5, -6.8), LCB=(7.5, -15.8),
                            RCB=(7.5, 15.8)), los=40, to_go=10)
pr2.highlight("FS", "SS")
fld = draw(pr2, lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 19.0))
widths(fld, pr2, -6.6)
plt.show()
```

**Closed or open? What coverage do the safeties' depth and width suggest, and where is this
defense thinnest against the pass?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Middle of the field open, and the shallow, narrow safeties point to quarters (Cover 4).** Cover 2
safeties would be deeper (12 to 14 yards) and wider (outside the hash, toward the numbers), because
each has half the field. These two are at 10 yards over the slots, the alignment of quarters
safeties, who guard only the inside quarter deep and read the slot receiver in front of them: if he
blocks or the play is a run, the safety comes downhill and becomes an extra run defender. That is
why defenses like quarters on first-and-10: two-high against the pass, with eight players who can
reach the run.

The thin spot is **underneath and outside**. Four deep leaves three underneath, so short throws to
the outside receivers (hitches and quick outs in front of the off corners) and to the flats are
open, and a safety reading the run is vulnerable to play-action behind him. What's hard is the
deep ball: four defenders in four narrow lanes. ([Quarters](06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd) shows
how its match rules handle the slot routes.)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-6, everybody tight"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-cover1
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-6. One safety (FS) 15 yards deep in the middle. Both corners (CB) pressed about a yard off the outside receivers, square to them; the nickel ($) pressed on the left slot; the strong safety (SS) 4 yards off the tight end Y in the right slot; the two linebackers inside. The corners and the free safety are ringed."
pr3 = Play(spread(), nickel(FS=(15.0, 0.0), SS=(4.0, 8.4), NB=(1.6, -8.4), LCB=(1.3, -15.7),
                            RCB=(1.3, 15.7), MIKE=(4.5, 1.2), WILL=(4.5, -2.4)), los=40, to_go=6)
pr3.highlight("FS", "LCB", "RCB")
fld = draw(pr3, lateral=(-22, 22), window=(-7.5, 19.0))
widths(fld, pr3, -6.6)
plt.show()
```

**Man or zone? What is the defense most likely playing, which routes should the quarterback
like, and what does the 5-yard rule have to do with it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Most likely man coverage with one deep safety: Cover 1.** Middle of the field closed, and every
receiver has a defender tight on him: corners pressed and square, the nickel pressed on H, the
strong safety close on Y. The linebackers likely have the back (and one may be free to rush or to
sit in the hole as a rat). On third-and-6 that's a common call: the defense wants every short throw
contested.

The quarterback should like **routes that beat man**: quick slants and outs that win at the break,
crossing routes and rubs that drag defenders through traffic ([Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)'s
mesh), and a back-shoulder throw against a corner in trail. He should not expect receivers to
"find a soft spot and sit," because there are no soft spots in man: sitting down next to your
defender just makes the throw harder. And the 5-yard rule is the receiver's friend: the corners get
one legal jam, inside 5 yards. A receiver who wins that first step has a defender chasing him with
his back to the quarterback, and only the free safety behind them. If the pressed corners bail at
the snap, it was a disguised zone and the quarterback has to adjust after the snap.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Every coverage is a decision about how many defenders to put deep.** Thirds (three deep, four
  under), halves (two deep, five under) and quarters (four deep, three under) each buy something
  and give something up; with four rushers, every defender added deep is one taken from underneath.
- **The underneath map is flat, curl, hook and hole.** There are always more areas than defenders,
  so zone players are taught to cover two areas each, and they drop to landmarks so the gaps are
  the planned size on every play.
- **How a defender lines up is a message.** Press contests timing and needs help deep; off coverage
  gives a cushion to protect against the deep ball; a bail makes zone look like man. Leverage tells
  you where his help is, and the 5-yard rule limits press to one legal jam.
- **There are three ways to guard a receiver:** spot-drop zone (run to a place, watch the
  quarterback), pattern matching (start as zone, pick up receivers by rule) and man (go with one
  receiver from the snap). Watch one underneath defender for one second and you can usually tell
  which.
- **Read the middle of the field.** Closed (one safety in the post) means Cover 1 or Cover 3 most of
  the time; open means a two-high coverage. Safety depth and width, corner depth and leverage, and
  slot alignment narrow it down, and the snap confirms or overturns it.
- **Coverage numbers count deep defenders through Cover 4, then become names.** Cover 6, 7, 8 and 9
  mean different things in different playbooks, and even charting services disagree.
